title: THE BIBLE CAN CONDEMN LUST AND CELEBRATE SEXUAL DESIRE—Because Those Are Not Automatically the Same Thing
paragraphs: THE BIBLE CAN CONDEMN LUST AND CELEBRATE SEXUAL DESIRE—Because Those Are Not Automatically the Same Thing

What if some Christians have spent years feeling ashamed of something God created good—not because Scripture called every form of sexual desire sinful, but because somewhere along the way we stopped distinguishing desire from coveting, intimacy from exploitation, and God's gift from humanity's corruption of it?
There are people reading this who learned to feel guilty before they ever learned to understand why.
Nobody had to catch them doing anything.
Sometimes all it took was attraction.
A feeling.
A heartbeat that suddenly became louder around someone beautiful.
And almost immediately, another voice arrived.
Dirty.
Sinful.
Lustful.
God must be disappointed in you.
So they prayed harder.
Looked away faster.
Felt ashamed longer.
Some eventually married and carried that shame straight into the bedroom.
The wedding happened.
The vows were spoken.
The covenant was real.
But somewhere inside, their conscience never received the message that something had changed.
Desire still felt suspicious.
Pleasure still felt vaguely unholy.
The body still felt like the enemy.
And perhaps nobody ever told them something astonishing:
The Bible that fiercely condemns sexual sin is also the Bible that can speak beautifully, poetically, and sometimes startlingly openly about sexual desire.
Not because Scripture contradicts itself.
Because lust and sexual desire are not automatically the same thing.
That distinction matters.
It matters to the unmarried Christian fighting temptation.
It matters to the husband who has quietly learned to associate desire with shame.
It matters to the wife who wonders whether enjoying her husband's desire somehow makes intimacy less spiritual.
It matters to the believer recovering from pornography.
It matters to the person carrying sexual wounds.
It matters to anyone who has confused holiness with becoming less human.
And it matters because Jesus did not come merely to teach us how to suppress ourselves.
He came to redeem us.
Including the parts of us sin has distorted.
Go back to the words of Christ that Christians often quote when talking about lust.
Matthew 5:28 in Greek reads:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.

Jesus is speaking about looking at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν—a looking directed toward desiring her in the context Jesus identifies as adultery in the heart. The verse does not reduce holiness to the biological impossibility of ever noticing that another human being is attractive. Christ takes the command against adultery inward, exposing the heart where sin can be cultivated before the body ever acts.
That is devastatingly important.
Because Jesus is not merely policing bodies.
He is exposing hearts.
Long before the Sermon on the Mount, the Ten Commandments had already reached into that territory.
Exodus 20:17 says:
לֹא תַחְמֹד אֵשֶׁת רֵעֶךָ
Lo taḥmod eshet re‘ekha.
“You shall not covet your neighbor's wife.”

The Hebrew verb חָמַד — ḥāmad can carry the sense of desiring, coveting, taking pleasure in, or regarding something as desirable. In Exodus 20:17 the object and context make the moral boundary unmistakable: this is desire reaching toward what belongs to another.
That is different from saying every experience of attraction is inherently sinful.
And Scripture itself proves why that distinction matters.
Because only a few books away from Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the prophets sits a book that has made generations of embarrassed Bible readers wonder how it survived the church committee.
Song of Songs.
Read it slowly and the myth that the Bible is embarrassed by marital desire becomes very difficult to maintain.
The lovers notice each other.
They long for each other.
They describe each other.
They delight in one another.
There is anticipation.
Beauty.
Exclusivity.
Longing.
Desire.
In Song of Songs 7, after language celebrating the beloved's physical beauty, we eventually hear:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani le-dodi, ve‘alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
The Hebrew word there is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah—desire, longing. The context is not pornography. It is not adultery. It is not exploitation. It is the poetry of lovers belonging to one another.
Notice what Scripture does not do.
It does not interrupt the poem to apologize for the human body.
God is not embarrassed that human beings have bodies.
He designed them.
Before pornography commercialized the body, God created it.
Before adultery betrayed covenant, God created covenant.
Before lust learned to consume people, God created people capable of loving and being loved.
Before sin distorted sexuality, sexuality existed within a creation God called good.
The enemy is not creativity.
Corruption is.
The enemy is not the existence of desire.
Sin is what desire can become when it stops loving the person and starts consuming the person.
That is where so much confusion begins.
Lust says, “Your body exists for my imagination.”
Love says, “You bear the image of God.”
Lust asks, “What can I take?”
Covenant asks, “How can I faithfully give?”
Lust can turn a person into pieces.
Love keeps seeing the whole person.
Lust wants pleasure detached from holiness, responsibility, covenant, and the good of the other person.
Biblical sexual desire within marriage can say, without shame, “I desire you”—while still honoring the beloved as a person rather than treating them as an object.
And Proverbs becomes astonishingly direct about this.
“May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
The Hebrew contains the imperative:
וּשְׂמַח — u-semaḥ.
Rejoice.
Not merely tolerate.
Not reluctantly endure.
Rejoice.

The context of Proverbs 5 contrasts marital faithfulness with forbidden sexual relationships, and the positive instruction directs sexual joy homeward into marriage. One translation note explicitly describes the passage as finding pleasure in a fulfilling marriage and treats that delight as God-given.
Then Paul says something equally remarkable to married Christians in Corinth.
μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους...
“Do not deprive one another...”

He allows temporary abstinence by mutual agreement for prayer, followed by reunion. Whatever else must be said about the passage—and it must never be twisted into permission for coercion—the language is reciprocal. Paul speaks to husband and wife about mutuality. Sexual intimacy in marriage is not portrayed as contamination from which spiritual people should permanently escape.
And in the very same New Testament, Paul can write:
τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας...
“This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
The Greek word is πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
Do you see the balance?
Scripture does not solve sexual brokenness by declaring sexuality itself broken.
It draws boundaries because something valuable exists inside those boundaries.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the home destroys it.
The answer is not to hate fire.
The answer is to understand what it is for.
And perhaps this is where the article stops being about Greek and Hebrew and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because maybe your problem isn't that you have never understood the word lust.
Maybe you understand it far too well.
Maybe you know exactly what it is like to look at another person and deliberately turn them into fantasy.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to consume bodies before your heart remembers they contain souls.
Maybe you promised God you would stop.
Then failed.
Promised again.
Failed again.
Deleted everything.
Downloaded it again.
Prayed.
Cried.
Fasted.
Fell.
And somewhere between repentance and relapse, you started wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want someone like you.
Listen carefully.
Do not rename your sin.
But do not rename the Savior either.
Sin is still sin.
Jesus is still Jesus.
And grace has never meant pretending darkness is light.
Grace means Christ entered our darkness to rescue sinners from it.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His mercy so extraordinary that He willingly came for sinners anyway.
That is why biblical conviction and biblical hope must remain together.
If your desire has become coveting, repent.
If pornography has trained you to consume human beings in your imagination, repent.
If you are entertaining someone else's spouse in your heart, repent.
If you have used another person's body without honoring their soul, repent.
If you are hiding an affair, repent.
If your secret sexual life would devastate the person sleeping beside you, stop calling secrecy protection.
Bring darkness into the light.
But hear the rest of the Gospel.
Repentance is not God standing at the door waiting to humiliate you.
Repentance is turning around because Someone is calling you home.
Jesus did not tell adulterers that adultery was beautiful.
He offered sinners something far more beautiful.
Mercy.
Forgiveness.
A new life.
The Gospel does not merely say, “Stop.”
It says, “Come.”
Come out of hiding.
Come out of pornography.
Come out of adultery.
Come out of shame.
Come out of self-righteousness.
Come out of the lie that because you have fallen repeatedly, Christ must finally be finished with you.
Come to the One whose blood is sufficient for sinners.
And maybe your story is different.
Maybe you are married and faithful, but you still feel guilty for desiring your spouse.
You don't need repentance for enjoying what God permits and blesses.
You may need healing from a distorted theology of the body.
Christian holiness does not require husbands and wives to pretend they are disembodied spirits.
The Bible can tell you to flee sexual immorality and tell you to rejoice in your spouse without contradiction.
Because holiness is not the destruction of desire.
It is the surrender of desire to God.
There are desires we crucify.
There are desires we discipline.
There are desires we refuse to feed.
There are desires we redirect.
And there are good gifts we receive with thanksgiving under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That distinction is everything.
Because Satan is happy with either distortion.
He can whisper, “Whatever you desire must be good.”
Or he can whisper, “The fact that you desire anything makes you dirty.”
Both lies can separate you from truth.
The first baptizes appetite.
The second demonizes embodiment.
Jesus does neither.
He calls us to holiness without teaching us to hate God's creation.
And that means the question is deeper than, “Did I feel desire?”
Ask what your desire is doing.
Is it honoring covenant or fantasizing about violating it?
Is it seeing a person or consuming an image?
Does it seek mutual love or selfish possession?
Does it move toward faithfulness or secrecy?
Can you bring it before Christ without needing to rewrite Scripture to justify it?
That last question hurts.
Because all of us are capable of becoming brilliant theologians when defending the thing we don't want to surrender.
But Jesus loves us too much to leave our chains unnamed.
And He loves us too much to call chains freedom.
Somebody reading this needs to stop hiding tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
You know what is on your phone.
You know the conversation you keep deleting.
You know the person whose profile you keep visiting.
You know the fantasy you keep feeding.
You know what your spouse doesn't know.
You know where innocent attraction crossed the line and became deliberate cultivation.
You know.
And Christ knows too.
Yet here you are.
Still reading.
Still breathing.
Still being called.
Grace has reached you again.
Not cheap grace that pats sin on the head.
Blood-bought grace that takes sinners to a cross, buries the old life, and raises people to walk differently.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of your private sin. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
No performance.
No pretending.
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of walking toward the light.
And please understand something else.
There are teenagers who desperately need this truth before pornography becomes their teacher.
There are married couples who need it before shame freezes what covenant was meant to protect.
There are single Christians who need to know that experiencing attraction does not give them permission to cultivate lust—but neither does attraction itself mean they have suddenly become filthy.
There are believers recovering from sexual sin who need someone to tell them that sanctification is possible.
There are people who have never entered a church because they assume Christians are either obsessed with sex or terrified of it.
Send it privately to someone who needs truth without public embarrassment.
Let your timeline become more than entertainment. Let it occasionally become a doorway through which somebody encounters Scripture, conviction, grace, and the name of Jesus Christ.
And for those asking how to help this ministry continue and expand, there is a practical way to stand with the work.
It doesn't.
Not because paying us is required to glorify God.
It isn't.
Your generosity before God is a matter of worship, stewardship, conscience, and biblical conviction.
But voluntary support for Gospel work can be a genuine act of generosity.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep putting Scripture where wounded people may find it at two in the morning.
Keep speaking about the subjects many people are afraid to touch.
Keep pointing scandalous stories toward redeeming grace.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, do not miss the greater invitation.
Give Christ your heart.
A donation cannot reconcile you to God.
A Christian T-shirt cannot make you holy.
A theological vocabulary cannot save you.
Jesus can.

The One who exposed adultery in the heart is also the One who went to the cross for adulterers, porn addicts, sexually broken people, religious hypocrites, ashamed spouses, secret sinners—and every other kind of sinner willing to come to Him.
The scandal is not that sinners need grace.
The scandal is how much grace Christ was willing to give.
So bring Him your sexuality.
Bring Him your desires.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him your singleness.
Bring Him the attraction you don't know what to do with.
Bring Him the habit you cannot seem to defeat.
Bring Him the shame you have carried for twenty years.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the nights nobody knows about.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the body you learned to hate.
Bring Him the heart you stopped trusting.
Bring Him everything.
And then stop asking Jesus merely to make you less tempted.
Ask Him to make you holy.
Ask Him to teach you how to see people as people again.
Ask Him to restore tenderness where pornography produced consumption.
Ask Him to restore trust where adultery produced devastation.
Ask Him to restore joy where shame poisoned marriage.
Ask Him to teach you that desire does not have to become your master.
Jesus is Lord.
Even here.
Especially here.
Maybe that is what somebody desperately needed to hear.
You are not called to worship your desires.
You are not called to obey every desire.
You are not called to pretend every desire is innocent.
But neither are you called to hate everything God created simply because sin learned how to corrupt it.
The answer to corrupted desire is not pretending we were never created to desire.
The answer is redemption.
Desire under Christ.
Bodies under Christ.
Marriage under Christ.
Singleness under Christ.
Sexuality under Christ.
Thoughts under Christ.
Eyes under Christ.
Everything under Christ.
Because Christianity is not Jesus receiving the religious-looking pieces of your life while you hide the embarrassing ones behind locked doors.
He wants the locked room too.
And when Jesus enters the room we were certain would make Him abandon us, we discover the heart of the Gospel:
He already knew what was inside.
He came anyway.
So save this for the night shame tries to rewrite your identity.
Share it with the person whose silence is getting dangerous.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or, if God has already brought you through this battlefield, tell someone there is hope.
Your testimony might become the sentence another person reads five minutes before deciding not to give up.
Because maybe the most dangerous lie shame ever told you was that Jesus would rewrite everybody's story except yours.
But the hand holding the pen still bears the scars.
